lawyer:
Md. Fazlul Karim, Advocate ------ For the Appellants. 
Kazi Shafiuddin Ahmed, Assistant Attorney General ------ For State.
parties:
Abdul Quddus & Another ------ Petitioner
Vs.
The State ------ Respondent
full_judgment:
6. Mr. Kazi Shafiuddin Ahmed, the learned Assistant Attorney General has argued that on the basis of the evidence on record it has been proved that the victim girl P.W.2 Ferdousi Begum was below the age of 16 years, that there is abundant evidence on record that P.W.2 was taken away by the appellants from the custody of her maternal grand-father P.W.4 Mokbul Hossain in whose custody she was lawfully entrusted (which comes within the ambit of the explanation of section 361 of the Penal Code) of which the accused appellants had sufficient notice and no prejudice on this ground was caused to the accused appellants, that it has also been proved by the prosecution that the accused appellants kidnapped the victim girl P.W.2 in order that she may be forced or seduced to illicit intercourse, that therefore the conviction of the appellants under section 366 of the Penal Code should be tip-held, that it has also been proved by the prosecution that the 2 accused appellants Abdul Quddus and Abul Hossain committed rape on P.W. 2 Ferdousi Begum against her will and without her consent and that therefore the conviction and sentence passed against the 2 accused appellants under section 376 of the Penal Code should be upheld, He argued that the decisions referred to by the learned advocate for the appellants are distinguishable inasmuch as they generally related to cases of married and mature women and even where it relates to minor unmarried girl it refers to cases of misdirection to the Jury for not cautioning them that they should consider whether it is reasonable and safe to act upon the evidence of the victim girl or women not corroborated by independent evidence. He refers to the decisions in the cases of Shah Alan) and others V. The Crown 10 D.L.R. 237 and Rameshwar V. The State of Rajasthan. (1952) S. C. R. (India) 377. In support of his argument that the question of corroboration by independent evidence arises generally in the case of a woman of full age he refers to the following observation made in the decision of the case of Momtaz Ahmed Khan V. The State 19 D.L.R. (S.C.) 259 (265): 

 "In certain jurisdictions, it is the rule that the solitary evidence of the prosecutrix being a woman of full age is not accepted as sufficient, but requires corroboration by independent evidence, in order to be believed." 

 10. The evidence of P.W.8 Dr. Mohammad Ali Sarkar, Radiologist and P.W. 11 Dr. G.M.A. Quader, Lecturer, Medical Jurisprudence, Rangpur Medical College has been discussed in detail in the judgment of the trial Court. P.W.8 Dr. Mohammad Ali Sarkar took X-Ray of various parts of the body of P.W.2 on 21-6-79 (X-Ray plates Ext. 4 series) and on the basis of the position of various joints opined that the skeletal age of P.W.2 was approximately 151 years. His X-Ray report is Ext. 3. He denied the defence suggestion that she was aged between 164 years to 17 years. He also denied the defence suggestion that he gave a perfunctory report on being influenced by tendered witness P.W. 7 Reazul Karim. P.W. 11 Dr. G.M.A. Quddus also examined P.W.2 on 21-6-79, saw the X-Ray plates Ext.4 series and opined that she was below the age of 16 years at that time. Accused appellant Abdul Quddus produced a medical certificate in his examination under section 342 Cr. P.C. The said medical certificate has been signed by someone with the date 19-5-79 above a seal in Bengali containing the words "Deputy Civil Sargeon, Bogra". In this medical certificate it has not been stated that police forwarded P.W.2 Ferdousi Begum whereupon she was being examined and it is also not the defence case that P.W.2 was forwarded to the alleged doctor at Bogra by the police. The certificate simply says that Miss Ferdousi Begum, daugher of late Fazlul Karim Tota Mia village chakundia, P.S. Gobindoganj, District Rangpur appeared before him on 19-5-79 for determination of her age, that her menstruation started 3 years back, that her weight was 102 lbs. and that on examination of various parts of her body he was of the opinion that the girl was aged about 17 years. The genuineness of this certificate by the Deputy Civil Surgeon, Bogra is very much in doubt. Moreover a doctor of the rank of a Deputy Civil Surgeon of the Government would not normally examine an unmarried girl without her being forwarded by the police and also would not give any opinion regarding her approximate age without any X-Ray report whatsoever merely on physical examination. The trial judge who had himself seen the girl P.W.2 after a thorough examination of the whole question of age has accepted the opinion of P.W.8 Dr. Mohammad Ali Sacker and P.W.11 Dr. G.M.A. Quader to the effect that the age of the girl P.W.2 Ferdousi Begum on 21-6-79 was less than 16 years. We also are of the opinion on the basis of the evidence on record that her age on the said date was below 16 years and we find no reason to differ with the view taken by the trial Court in this regard, especially in view of the fact that the trial Court also had the opportunity of seeing the girl (P.W.2) in Court. 

 12. It is in evidence that accused appellant Abdul Quddus, aged more than 40 years has two wives. It is also undisputed that lie has six children. In such circumstances even if it was true that P.W.2 had written these letters earlier to the kidnapping site being an immature and unmarried minor girl was obviously duped and deceived and she was made to think that accused appellant Quddus Nausha really would keep her in a separate house in Gaibandha as his legally married wife but accused appellant Quddus and his brother-in-law accused appellant Abul Hossain (aged more than 38 years) had other nefarious plans. They took full advantage of the innocence and simplicity of this minor girl P.W.2 Ferdousi Bcgum, kidnapped her in the night of occurrence from the custody of her grandfather P.W.4 Mokbul Hossain with intent that she may be compelled and forced to have illicit intercourse with them and that both the accused appellants Abdul Quddus and Abul Hossain actually raped her forcibly against her will and without her con-sent in village Behargili in the house of appellant Abul Hossain's brother-in-law Sirajul Islam. The said affidavit, the true copy of nikanama and the medical certificate produced by accused appellant Abdul Quddus also go to corroborate the testimony of P.W.2 Ferdousi that after kidnapping her from the custody of her grandfather with intent to commit illicit intercourse with her and after boils the accused appellant had raped her against her will and without her consent by force, they tried to obtain documents to show that there was a marriage between appellant Quddus and P.W.2 Ferdousi subsequently at the office of the marriage Registrar, Chelopara, Bogra on 19-5-79, in the Court of a Magistrate at Bogra on 4-6-79 and that P.W.2 Ferdousi was aged about 17 years. 

 13. In the case of Shah Alain and others V. The Crown 10 D.L.R. 237 it was observed, "We are not prepared to hold that the rule (the rule of prudence that the evidence of the prosecutrix alone should not be acted upon unless substantially corroborated by other evidence) applies with equal rigidity in cases which were not strictly cases of sexual offences. A case of abduction or kidnapping only is not, in our view a case of a sexual offence, and we respectfully agree with Chief Justice Beaumont that the rule does not apply to an offence under section 366." 

 14. The leading case on the rule of prudence that the evidence of the prosecutrix or the complainant in sexual offences or unnatural offences should generally be corroborated by some other evidence direct or circumstantial before it is acted upon is the decision in the case of The King V. Baskerville (1916) 2 K.B. 658. The prisoner in that case was tried for committing unnatural offences with two boys who were freely consenting parties and there was no use of force. The only direct evidence of the acts charged was that of the boys themselves who on their own statement were accomplices in the offence. The prisoner gave evidence and admitted that the boys came to his flat by his invitation but explained it away by saying that the boys who were poor were invited from philanthropic motives. A letter addressed to one of the boys containing a ten shilling Treasury note inviting both the boys to come to his place was produced and it was admitted by the prisoner to be in his hand writing. The judge warned the jury that they ought not to convict the prisoner upon the evidence of the boys unless it was corroborated in some material particulars affecting the accused, but told them that the above mentioned letter afforded evidence which they would be entitled to find to be sufficient corroboration. The jury found the prisoner guilty. The court of Criminal Appeal dismissed the appeal. Lord Reading, the Lord Chief Justice to England delivering the judgment of the Special Bench upheld the conviction. In this case the letter was considered to be sufficient corroboration. Even where there is no corroborative evidence, the jury is free to rely on the evidence of the victim of a sexual offence. Only thing that is necessary is that the judge should duly caution the jury of the danger of convicting a prisoner on the uncorroborated testimony of an accomplice but simultaneously the judge should also point out to the jury that it is within legal province to convict upon such uncorroborated evidence. The same principles apply in the case of trial by a judge without the aid of jury, Lord Reading observed. 

 Lord Reading further observed that it would be in a high degree dangerous to attempt to formulate the kind of evidence which would be regarded as corroboration, except to say that corroborative evidence is evidence which shows or tends to show that the story of the accomplice that the accused committed the crime is true not merely that the crime has been committed, but that it was committed by the accused. The corroboration need not be direct evidence that the accused committed the crime; it is sufficient if it is merely circumstantial evidence of his connection with the crime. Lord Reading observed. 

 15. While considering the question of the necessity of corroboration of the evidence of a girl or woman who is said to have been raped, in all circumstances it cannot be said that she is an accomplice. In cases where she is not a freely consenting party and not an accomplice, if she was abducted by deceitful means or by force or if she was ravished against her will and without her consent, she is not an accomplice. In such circumstances she is a victim of an outrage. On the basis of the facts of each case the trial Court has to come to a finding whether it is safe to act upon the testimony of the complainant without being supported by independent corroborative evidence. This view finds support in the decision in the case of Rameshwar V. The State of Rajasthan, 1952 S.C.R. (India) 377. 

 16. Although section 133 of the Evidence Act provides that an accomplice shall be a competent witness against the accused persons and the conviction is not illegal merely because it proceeds upon the uncorroborated testimony of an accomplice, yet illustration (b) to section 114 of the Evidence Act is the rule of guidance to which the court should have due regard. The said illustration (b) provides that the Court may presume that the accomplice is unworthy of credit unless he is corroborated in material particulars. The law and the rule of prudence are certainly not higher in the case of sexual offences. In the case of a trial by a judge without the aid of jury it is necessary for the judge to express in his judgment that this rule of caution is in his mind and in case the judge decides to accept the uncorroborated testimony of the victim girl or woman, he should state the reasons why he considers it safe to convict the accused without any corroborative evidence. 

 17. The previous statement of a victim girl after the alleged commission of the offence was considered to be legally admissible as evidence of conduct in the decision in the case of Rameshwar V. The State of Rajasthan, 1952 S.C.R. (India) 377 in view of the provisions of section 157 and Illustration (j) to section 8 of the Evidence Act which is as follows: 

 Section 157 of the Evidence Act reads as follows: "In order to corroborate the testimony of a witness, any former statement made by such witness relating to the same fact at or about the time when the fact took place, or before any authority legally competent to investigate the fact, may be proved." 

 18. There is thus no doubt that such a statement made by a victim girl or woman after the occurrence is legally admissible as corroboration. The value and weight to be attached to such corroboration is a different matter and in cases where the prosecutrix is an accomplice or is found to be coming out with a false and concocted story with an ill motive or at the instance of someone else, it may be said that tainted evidence does not lose its taint merely by repetition. It all depends on the facts of each case. So far as section 157 of the Evidence Act is concerned, it may be said that the English Law on this point is different and does not admit such statements into evidence. 

 20. In this case we have shown that apart from the evidence of P.W.2 Ferdousi Begum accused appellant Abdul Quddus @ Nausha has produced the medical certificate, the true copy of nikanama and the affidavit to show that after P.W.2 went away with them, she was married to hint at Bogra and that a certificate showing the age of P.W.2 to be 17 years was obtained from a doctor. These facts independently connect the two accused appellants with the crime. P.W.3 and P.W.4 also state that in the night of occurrence P.W.2 was found missing from their house and they do not state that the two appellants took P.W.2 away with their consent. P.W.4 Mokbul Hossain made G.D. Entry No 83 dated 4-5-79 at Gavindaganj P.S. These facts also independently corroborate the evidence of P.W.2 Ferdousi Begum. Immediately after she was recovered by the police she was taken to P.W. 10 Mr. M.A. Shukur before whom she on 19-6-79 made statement Ext. 2 which corroborates her present statement. P.W.11 Dr. Quader on physical examination of P.W.2 Ferdousi on 21-6-79 opined that she was raped. No unmarried minor girl aged below 16 years would voluntarily agree to marry a man of more than 40 years having two wives, 5 daughters and a son and in the facts and circumstances of the present case voluntarily agree to have sexual intercourse with accused appellants Quddus and Abul Hossain. These facts also go to corroborate the evidence of P.W.2. Therefore it is not correct to say that the evidence of P.W.2 is not corroborated by any other independent evidence. 

 21. There is no substance in the argument that the accused appellants were prejudiced as they were not told in the charge under section 366A of the Penal Code that P.W.2 Ferdousi Begum was taken away from the custody of her maternal grandfather P.W.4 Mokbul Hossain. We have already shown that there is sufficient evidence on record to show that P.W. 2 Ferdousi was residing with her maternal grand-father P.W.4 Mokbul Hossain at the time of occurrence and that she was taken away from the house of her maternal grandfather P.W. 4 Mokbul by the two accused appellants in the night of occurrence. The accused appellants therefore had sufficient notice of the fact that they had taken away P.W.2 Ferdousi Begum from the custody of P. W.4 Mokbul Hossain who within the ambit of the explanation in section 361 of the Penal Code was the lawfully entrusted guardian of the victim girl P.W.2 Ferdousi at the time of occurrence. The accused has not been prejudiced in any manner in the matter of framing of the charge under section 366A of the Penal Code and the offence under section 366 of the Penal Code is minor to the offence under section 366A of the Penal Code. 

 22. From the discussion of the evidence, circumstance and facts on record we find that P.W.2 Ferdousi Begum aged below 16 years was kidnapped by the two appellants Abdul Quddus and Abul Hossain with intent that she may be forced or compelled to have illicit intercourse with them and it has also been proved beyond reasonable doubts that the two accused appellants raped her against her will and without her consent forcibly. The defence suggestion that P.W.1 Wahedul Islam wanted 5 bighas of land and his taxi to be transferred to the nana of the P.W.2 Ferdousi Begum and that as he (appellant Quddus) did not agree to the proposal wholly, the two accused appellants have been falsely implicated in this case has been denied by P.W.1 Wahedul Islam and no other witness has admitted such suggestion. The defence case that P.W.2 Ferdousi Begum was aged 17 years, that she married accused appellant Quddus voluntarily and that the prosecution case regarding kidnapping and rape is false has also not become probable in any manner. We have already shown that the prosecution has proved the charges under sections 366 and 376 of the Penal Code against the accused appellants Abdul Quddus @Nausha and Abul Hossain beyond reasonable doubts. They have therefore been rightly convicted thereunder.
